idiom_name: policy object returning std::optional / std::expected; [[nodiscard]] decision consumed at the call site
implementation_notes: The standard library contains no authorization layer, so the rule is hand-written: a policy type answers a query for (subject, operation, resource) and returns a value only when an explicit grant matched - `std::optional<Grant>` from C++17 or `std::expected<Grant, Deny>` from C++23 - so an empty optional or an error is the denial and the type expresses 'no answer' instead of a boolean that needs a convention. Mark the decision `[[nodiscard]]` and deny on the empty case at the call site; the compiler then warns when a decision is dropped, but it does not force the branch, so the deny remains a review point. Where the operation must be impossible without a grant, make it unconstructible: a scoped guard/capability object whose constructor takes the decision and whose methods are the only route to the resource carries the rule into the type system.
pitfalls: A default-initialized `std::optional` contains no value, which is a convenient denial - but code that treats an `optional<bool>` or an engaged-but-meaningless value as the answer reintroduces the ambiguity: contain a Grant, not a bool.

`*optional` without a check is undefined behaviour and `value()` throws `bad_optional_access`; a broad `catch (...)` around the decision that continues is the C++ fail-open path - translate exceptions into a denial instead.
Permissive initializers are the same failure in different syntax: `bool allowed = true;`, an `operator bool` on a policy object that defaults to true, or `value_or(Grant::all())`.

Global or static policy registries have non-deterministic initialization order across translation units: a guard that reads an empty map because the registry is not constructed yet must treat 'policy unavailable' as a denial, not as 'no restrictions configured'.
